Q: ARM MTE synchronous mode: what does “store must complete tag check before next store executes” mean? A:

So what exactly are you suggesting, that sync-MTE forces in-order exec of store instructions (of writing to the store buffer) to prevent timing side-channels (like used to exploit Spectre) with store-forwarding to code that runs in the shadow of some kind of mis-speculation?

Ok, interesting, non-sync mode doesn't raise exceptions at all for tag-check failure, only sets a flag which the kernel can check later. So exceptions are always precise, but async mode doesn't have one possible source of exceptions.

I don't really get why a tag-check exception would be different from any other possible fault (like a page fault) on a store, in terms of maintaining precise exceptions. If a store is marked as faulting (e.g. bad address), it will do that when trying to retire, so its store-buffer entry won't commit to L1d cache. And neither will any younger stores. Any older loads won't have forwarded from it (by definition), and any younger loads will be discarded when rolling back to a consistent retirement state when taking the fault. (Assuming the faulting store reaches retirement, rather than being discarded if some earlier mispredict or exception is discovered.)

So if a uarch can do out-of-order exec and/or commit of stores normally, I don't see why sync-MTE would need to stop that. Perhaps only for extra security against speculation-based attacks?

BTW, this is ARM not Intel, so "issue" is the right word for sending an instruction or uop from the scheduler to an execution unit.

Also, normally a store-buffer entry would be allocated for a store instruction during alloc/rename ("dispatch" in non-Intel terminology). (I think on CPUs that support misaligned stores, the same SB entry handles the whole data. It's up to the commit stage to split it between cache lines, I think, rather than allocating a second SB entry during exec.) On x86 CPUs where commit from the store-buffer has to be in-order, program-order alloc of SB entries should normally make finding a free entry just advancing a pointer in a ring buffer like in the ROB (reorder buffer). I've often wondered how weakly-ordered CPUs manage this, whether they reclaim out of order as well, or if they can't re-allocate past the oldest not-yet-committed store.
(That seems likely, and same for x86 CPUs with NT stores. Checking all entries in parallel to find a free one would be more power-intensive. It would mean that you stall if even one cache-miss store is outstanding for too long, but in practice IDK how common it to have a handful of cache-miss stores followed by a lot of cache-hit stores.)

Anyway, I'm pretty sure load and store buffer entries would only get allocated while moving an instruction/uop from the front-end to the back-end. (Dispatch / rename / allocate.) Same for physical register entries, branch-order-buffer entries, and pretty much anything else. In-order allocation makes things much simpler, and means that a resource stall stalls the front-end rather than execution on a certain back-end port.

(Write buffers for flushing a cache line from L1d to outer levels of cache / RAM can be allocated on demand as needed, since they aren't a resource necessary for an instruction to execute. Like LFBs in Intel uarches.)

Q: Do I need to update the version if changes have been made to CMake for the library? A:

What have you changed in the library's externally-accessible API? What can or must consumers of your library change in order to use the updated library or your newly-added features?

These map directly to the standard semantic versioning rules. If you changed your own build system, but your consumers don't need to change anything (the same -I, -L, -l compiler options work the same way) then it's only a patch-version update, 1.2.3 -> 1.2.4.

Q: Android Automotive: Detected if trailer is connected A:

To access the TRAILER_PRESENT vehicle property, the app must be granted the Car.PERMISSION_PRIVILEGED_CAR_INFO permission. This is a signature, privileged permission which means the Android build has to include your app in the privileged permission allowlist.

Q: Permission denied on \o A:

\o file.html creates the file on the machine where psql is running, in the current working directory of that psql session. Permission denied is an operating system permission issue, not a PostgreSQL/SQL issue.

Check where you are writing:

\! pwd

Then either change to a writable directory:

\cd /path/you/can/write
\H
\o orders.html
SELECT * FROM orders;
\o

or give an absolute path:

\H
\o /home/your_user/orders.html
SELECT * FROM orders;
\o

The final \o with no filename turns output redirection off.

If you are using an online/web terminal or restricted environment, it may not allow writing files in the current directory. In that case, choose a writable directory such as your home directory or download/export the result using the tool’s UI.

Q: Styled Components & React: Click event A:

Your span is rendered with a css value of display: inline. If there is no actual content in it to expand, it will be 0 pixels in width, and therefore you are not actually clicking on it.

I ran into the same issues and in Styled Components I couldn't make it work with a forced display: block. You should use a clickable item, like styled.button...

Q: Unable to get permission android.car.permission.CAR_MILLAGE_3P A:

Car.PERMISSION_MILEAGE_3P was introduced in Android 16 so vehicles running on older versions will not use this permission.
